section_1a.directions: Section I, Part A — Multiple Choice: 55 questions, 55 minutes. Each question is followed by four answer choices. Select the choice that best answers the question or completes the statement. This part counts for 40 percent of the exam score. Work briskly; all questions count equally.

items.stem: MacDougall's argument most directly helps explain which of the following later developments in Spain?
options: (A) Spain's rise as the leading industrial power of seventeenth-century Europe.
(B) The widening gap between Spain's wealthy elite and its impoverished majority during the 1600s.
(C) Spain's decisive and lasting naval domination over its European rivals in the seventeenth century.
(D) The successful revolts of Spain's American colonies against imperial rule in the seventeenth century.
items.explanation: The flood of American silver into Spain enriched the crown and a narrow elite of merchants and officials while driving up prices across the kingdom. Ordinary Spaniards faced inflation that eroded wages, and productive industry withered as easy bullion wealth made manufacturing uncompetitive. The result was a seventeenth-century Spain split between a wealthy few and an impoverished many — exactly the widening gap MacDougall's argument explains.

option_explanations.A: Wrong. Spain did not become the leading industrial power of the 1600s; its industry stagnated while Northern Europe industrialized.
option_explanations.B: Correct. New World wealth concentrated among Spain's elite while inflation and economic decline impoverished the majority, widening the rich-poor gap.
option_explanations.C: Wrong. Spain's naval power declined in the 1600s — the Armada's defeat came in 1588, and Dutch and English sea power rose afterward.
option_explanations.D: Wrong. Spain's American colonies did not successfully revolt in the seventeenth century; independence came in the early 1800s.

items.stem: The map above — Martin Waldseemuller's 1507 world map, the first to apply the name 'America' to the New World — best supports which of the following conclusions?

stimulus.image_caption: Martin Waldseemuller, Universalis Cosmographia, 1507 — the first map to name 'America.'
stimulus.pd_rationale: Martin Waldseemuller, 1507; pre-1930

options: (A) Europeans had fully mapped the Pacific coastline of the Americas by 1507.
(B) The name 'America' honored the Spanish monarchs who financed transatlantic exploration.
(C) Europeans had come to recognize the lands across the Atlantic as a distinct continent rather than part of Asia.
(D) Waldseemuller's map was commissioned to fix the Treaty of Tordesillas boundary between Spain and Portugal.
items.explanation: Waldseemuller's 1507 map gave the New World its own name — America — and drew it as a separate landmass. That choice shows Europeans had stopped treating these lands as the eastern edge of Asia, as Columbus had insisted, and had begun to understand them as a distinct fourth continent. The naming itself marks the conceptual breakthrough.

option_explanations.A: Wrong. The 1507 map did not show a fully charted Pacific coast; Europeans were still guessing at the continent's western extent.
option_explanations.B: Wrong. The name honored the explorer Amerigo Vespucci, whose accounts described the new lands — not the Spanish monarchs.
option_explanations.C: Correct. Naming the lands America and mapping them separately shows Europeans now recognized a distinct continent rather than part of Asia.
option_explanations.D: Wrong. The map was a scholar's publication celebrating new geographic knowledge, not a diplomatic tool for the Tordesillas boundary.

items.stem: Which one of the following statements about the Spanish conquest of the Americas is most accurate?

stimulus.text: Source 1: “He who is by nature not his own but another’s man, is by nature a slave; and he may be said to be another’s man who, being a human being, is also a possession.” Source: Aristotle, Politics, Book I (c. 350 BCE; Benjamin Jowett translation, 1885 — public domain). Source 2: Paraphrased from Mary Ann Glendon, “The Forgotten Crucible: The Latin American Influence on the Universal Human Rights Idea” (2003). Glendon argues that as Latin American nations gained independence in the nineteenth century, two intellectual strains merged with an older, more universalist natural-law tradition to produce a distinctively Latin American discourse of rights. She traces its roots to the Spanish Dominicans — above all Bartolomé de Las Casas, the sixteenth-century bishop who condemned slavery and defended Native peoples on the basis of a natural right to liberty grounded in a single common humanity: “All the peoples of the world are humans,” Las Casas wrote, “and all the races of humankind are one.” Following Paolo Carozza and Brian Tierney, Glendon credits Las Casas and his fellow Dominicans with laying the groundwork for a doctrine of natural rights independent of religious revelation, drawn instead from human rationality and free will and from Aristotelian philosophy.

options: (A) African slavery was a direct result of Spanish settlements in Florida.
(B) Early native civilizations in Mexico introduced Spanish explorers to cattle ranching and wheat cultivation.
(C) Christopher Columbus was not the first European to have explored North America.
(D) Because of racial prejudice, Spanish explorers shunned intermarriage with native people.
items.explanation: The Norse reached North America around the year 1000 — Leif Erikson's settlement at L'Anse aux Meadows in Newfoundland predates Columbus by five centuries. Archaeological evidence confirms a Norse presence long before 1492. So while Columbus's voyages launched sustained European contact, he was not the first European to reach the continent.

option_explanations.A: Wrong. African slavery in the Americas grew out of the labor demands of sugar plantations in Brazil and the Caribbean, not from Spanish settlements in Florida.
option_explanations.B: Wrong. Cattle ranching and wheat were European introductions to the Americas, not practices Spaniards learned from native civilizations.
option_explanations.C: Correct. Norse explorers reached North America around 1000 CE, centuries before Columbus.
option_explanations.D: Wrong. Spanish colonists frequently intermarried with native peoples, producing the large mestizo population of colonial Latin America.

items.stem: In Britain's eyes, the chief economic function of the American colonies was The c. 1780s watercolor above shows a plantation producing staple crops with enslaved labor — the colonial economy Britain valued.

stimulus.image_caption: 'The Old Plantation,' watercolor of enslaved people on a South Carolina plantation, c. 1780s.
stimulus.pd_rationale: c.1780s watercolor, attributed American artist; pre-1930

options: A. To make manufactured goods England preferred not to produce
B. To grow staple crops such as tobacco
C. To supply raw materials such as lumber
D. Both B and C
items.explanation: Under mercantilism, Britain saw the colonies as an economic resource for the mother country. Their chief function was to supply what England needed: staple crops like tobacco, rice, and indigo grown on plantations, and raw materials like lumber, tar, and furs from forests and frontiers. Manufacturing finished goods was discouraged — that was England's job. The watercolor of enslaved laborers producing staple crops shows exactly the colonial economy Britain wanted.

option_explanations.A: Wrong. Britain wanted manufacturing kept in England; the colonies were not supposed to make the goods England preferred to produce itself.
option_explanations.B: True, but only part of the answer. Staple crops like tobacco were central, but so were raw materials.
option_explanations.C: True, but only part of the answer. Raw materials like lumber were central, but so were staple crops.
option_explanations.D: Correct. The colonies' chief economic function was both: growing staple crops such as tobacco and supplying raw materials such as lumber.

items.stem: What underlying Puritan belief made it possible for magistrates to fine the merchant in 1639 even though no statute authorized the penalty?

stimulus.text: Although some Puritan values resembled the rising capitalist ethic, Puritan economic life remained closer to the medieval than the modern. Unrestrained economic individualism would have alarmed any respectable Puritan. The statute books and court records of seventeenth-century Massachusetts are full of government-set price and wage controls. Puritans treated wealth as a trust from God, stressing duties and responsibilities alongside the benefits of work and gain. In 1639 the colony's General Court fined one of its richest merchants for excessive profiteering — though no statute prohibited the practice. The Puritans never separated religion from business and kept repeating the medieval idea of the 'just price.' Over the long run, though, once the Puritan work ethic was divorced from its religious setting, it quickened the spirit of capitalism: the old restraints on the individual gradually gave way to the enterprising, self-made figure who rose by his own exertions. — adapted from Gerald N. Grob and Robert N. Beck, American Ideas (1963)

options: (A) Wealth was a trust from God carrying communal obligations, so norms of a 'just price' and 'just wage' could override the absence of written law.
(B) Puritan courts held that magistrates could invent new laws whenever the colony's treasury ran short of funds.
(C) The General Court believed wealthy merchants were secretly working as agents of the Anglican hierarchy.
(D) Puritans held that English common law automatically permitted any penalty a magistrate chose to impose.
items.explanation: The Puritans believed wealth was a trust from God, carrying duties to the community alongside the right to profit. Their economy still followed the medieval idea of the just price — that prices and wages should be fair, not whatever the market would bear. That belief let the General Court punish excessive profiteering as a moral offense even with no statute on the books: the merchant had violated God's trust, and the magistrates enforced the community's moral norms.

option_explanations.A: Correct. Puritans treated wealth as a divine trust with communal obligations, so just-price norms could justify punishment even without a written statute.
option_explanations.B: Wrong. The fine was not about filling the treasury; it enforced the Puritan moral economy against profiteering.
option_explanations.C: Wrong. There is no evidence the merchant was accused of serving the Anglican hierarchy; the issue was excessive profit.
option_explanations.D: Wrong. Puritans did not believe magistrates could impose any penalty at will; the fine rested on shared religious norms about fair dealing, not arbitrary power.

items.stem: Which European colonists maintained the most cooperative relations with Native Americans?

stimulus.image_caption: Jacques-Nicolas Bellin, 'Carte de la partie orientale de la Nouvelle France,' 1744.
stimulus.pd_rationale: Jacques-Nicolas Bellin, 1744; pre-1930

options: A. The Spanish
B. The Dutch
C. The French
D. The English
items.explanation: The French came to North America mainly for the fur trade, which required Native cooperation — French traders lived among Native peoples, learned their languages, and forged alliances through trade and intermarriage. Unlike the Spanish encomienda system or English settler expansion that displaced tribes, the French economic model depended on partnership. That dependence produced the most cooperative — though still unequal and self-interested — relationship of any European colonists.

option_explanations.A: Wrong. Spanish relations were defined by conquest, forced labor, and missionary coercion — not cooperation.
option_explanations.B: Wrong. The Dutch had limited, mostly commercial contact centered on New Netherland and did not build the broad alliances the French did.
option_explanations.C: Correct. The French fur trade depended on Native partners, producing the most cooperative relations of any European colonists.
option_explanations.D: Wrong. English settler colonies expanded onto Native lands, producing repeated displacement and warfare.

items.stem: Smith's description of Powhatan as an 'emperor' surrounded by 'courtiers' most directly reveals that

stimulus.text:
Questions 21–24 refer to the following quotation.

"At last they brought him to Werowocomoco, where was Powhatan, their emperor. Here more than two hundred of those grim courtiers stood wondering at him..."
—Captain John Smith, on his capture, 1608 (abridged)

options: A. Powhatan had studied European government
B. Smith was fluent in Algonquian languages
C. Smith imposed European political categories on a Native society
D. The English recognized Powhatan sovereignty as fully equal
items.explanation: Powhatan led a powerful Algonquian chiefdom, but emperor and courtiers are European court vocabulary — titles from a world of kings and palaces. Smith reached for the only political language he knew, dressing a Native leader in the costume of European monarchy. The description tells us more about Smith's mental framework than about how Powhatan's society actually governed itself.

option_explanations.A: Wrong. There is no evidence Powhatan studied European government; the European terms are Smith's, not Powhatan's.
option_explanations.B: Wrong. The passage shows Smith using English political vocabulary, not demonstrating fluency in Algonquian.
option_explanations.C: Correct. Smith imposed European political categories — emperor, courtiers — on a Native society organized on entirely different terms.
option_explanations.D: Wrong. Using royal titles did not mean the English accepted Powhatan as a sovereign equal; they soon moved to dominate his people.

items.stem: The speech was delivered in the context of

stimulus.text:
Questions 13–16 refer to the following excerpt.

"I appeal to any white man to say if ever he entered Logan's cabin hungry and he gave him not meat... During the course of the last long and bloody war Logan remained idle in his cabin, an advocate for peace... I had even thought to have lived with you but for the injuries of one man. Colonel Cresap, the last spring, in cold blood and unprovoked, murdered all the relations of Logan... There runs not a drop of my blood in the veins of any living creature. This called on me for revenge. I have sought it. I have killed many... But do not harbor a thought that mine is the joy of fear. Logan never felt fear."
—Logan (Tah-gah-jute), speech recorded 1774 (abridged)

options: A. Pontiac's Rebellion against British rule in the Great Lakes region
B. King Philip's War between colonists and Native peoples in New England
C. Bacon's Rebellion against Virginia's colonial government in 1676
D. Lord Dunmore's War and escalating settler–Native conflict in the Ohio Valley
items.explanation: Logan's speech — recorded in 1774 — mourns his family murdered by Colonel Cresap's men and vows revenge. The context is Lord Dunmore's War: Virginia settlers pushing into the Ohio Valley, Cresap's unprovoked killings, and the cycle of retaliation that followed. Logan, a Mingo leader who had advocated peace, took up the hatchet only after his kin were slaughtered in cold blood.

option_explanations.A: Wrong. Pontiac's Rebellion (1763) was a Great Lakes uprising a decade earlier, not the 1774 Ohio Valley conflict Logan describes.
option_explanations.B: Wrong. King Philip's War (1675–1676) was fought in New England, a century's distance from Logan's Ohio country.
option_explanations.C: Wrong. Bacon's Rebellion (1676) was Virginians rebelling against their own governor, not Logan's war of revenge.
option_explanations.D: Correct. The speech belongs to Lord Dunmore's War and the escalating settler-Native violence in the Ohio Valley in 1774.

items.stem: Consistent with his speech, Patrick Henry would have been identified at the time as a(n)

stimulus.image_caption: Benjamin Franklin, 'Join, or Die,' Pennsylvania Gazette, May 9, 1754.
stimulus.pd_rationale: Benjamin Franklin, 1754; pre-1930
stimulus.stimulus_replacement: The image above: Franklin's 'Join, or Die' cartoon of May 9, 1754.

options: (A) loyalist
(B) conservative
(C) radical
(D) isolationist
items.explanation: Patrick Henry's Give me liberty or give me death speech was a call for armed resistance to Britain — the most radical position available in 1775. Moderates still hoped for reconciliation and conservatives defended the imperial connection; Henry demanded the colony mobilize for war. His contemporaries understood him as a radical: a man pushing beyond reform toward revolution.

option_explanations.A: Wrong. A loyalist defended the Crown; Henry demanded resistance to it.
option_explanations.B: Wrong. Conservatives of the day counseled caution and reconciliation; Henry demanded immediate military preparation.
option_explanations.C: Correct. Henry's call for armed resistance identified him as a radical in 1775.
option_explanations.D: Wrong. Isolationism concerns foreign entanglements; Henry's speech was about resisting British rule, not avoiding alliances.

items.stem: Washington's letter implies that the remedy for the crisis he describes is

stimulus.text:
The following questions refer to the excerpt below.

"I feel myself exceedingly obliged to you for the full & friendly communications in your letters... Commotions of this sort, like snow-balls, gather strength as they roll, if there is no opposition in the way to divide and crumble them."
—George Washington to Henry Knox on Shays's Rebellion, 1786 (abridged)

options: A. Appeasing the insurgents by granting their demands
B. A government strong enough to enforce its laws
C. Disbanding the state governments entirely
D. Appealing to Britain for military assistance
items.explanation: Washington watched Shays's Rebellion — armed Massachusetts farmers shutting down courts — and concluded that a government unable to suppress such commotions was no government at all. His snowball image makes the point: disorders gather strength unless met with force. The remedy he implies is a national government strong enough to enforce its laws and put down insurrection, which is why he soon supported the Constitutional Convention.

option_explanations.A: Wrong. Washington did not counsel appeasing the rebels; he wanted their commotion divided and crumbled by opposition.
option_explanations.B: Correct. Washington implies the crisis demands a government strong enough to enforce its laws against rebellion.
option_explanations.C: Wrong. Washington wanted stronger government, not the abolition of state governments.
option_explanations.D: Wrong. Appealing to Britain for help was unthinkable to Washington — the rebellion's whole point was American self-government.

items.stem: The cartoon's hope that the imperial crisis could still be resolved peacefully was most similarly expressed in which of the following?

stimulus.image_caption: 'The Colonies Reduc'd' (companion to Franklin's 'Magna Britannia: Her Colonies Reduc'd'), after Benjamin Franklin, published 1768.
stimulus.pd_rationale: After Benjamin Franklin, published by John Almon, 1768; British Museum, pre-1930

options: (A) Paul Revere's 1770 engraving of the Boston Massacre, which inflamed anti-British feeling.
(B) The 1768 Treaty of Fort Stanwix, which redrew the boundary with the Iroquois.
(C) The Olive Branch Petition of 1775, professing loyalty while seeking reconciliation.
(D) Thomas Paine's Common Sense (1776), which demanded immediate independence.
items.explanation: The Olive Branch Petition, sent to King George III in July 1775, professed the colonists' loyalty and begged him to restore peace — a final attempt at reconciliation even as fighting had begun at Lexington and Bunker Hill. Like the cartoon's hope for a peaceful settlement, it shows that many colonists still wanted the imperial crisis resolved without a complete break. Both express the reconciliation impulse of 1775, before independence became the goal.

option_explanations.A: Wrong. Revere's Boston Massacre engraving inflamed anti-British anger; it did not express hope for peaceful resolution.
option_explanations.B: Wrong. The Treaty of Fort Stanwix redrew a Native boundary line; it had nothing to do with reconciling Britain and the colonies.
option_explanations.C: Correct. The Olive Branch Petition of 1775 professed loyalty while seeking reconciliation — the same peaceful hope the cartoon expresses.
option_explanations.D: Wrong. Common Sense demanded immediate independence, the opposite of hoping for a peaceful imperial settlement.

items.stem: Which of the following specific developments best illustrates the 'national humiliation' Hamilton describes?
options: (A) Britain's refusal to evacuate its Great Lakes forts after the Treaty of Paris (1783).
(B) Spain's military reconquest of Florida from the United States.
(C) French-backed raids by Native allies on New England settlements.
(D) Dutch demands that American merchant ships pay tribute payments in order to dock in Holland.
items.explanation: After the Treaty of Paris (1783), Britain kept its troops in forts around the Great Lakes, within territory the treaty had ceded to the United States. To Hamilton and other nationalists, this was a humiliation: the victorious republic could not even compel a defeated Britain to leave its own soil. The forts' continued occupation proved the Confederation government's weakness to the world.

option_explanations.A: Correct. Britain's refusal to evacuate its Great Lakes forts after 1783 was the concrete humiliation Hamilton had in mind — foreign troops on American soil the government could not remove.
option_explanations.B: Wrong. Spain did not militarily reconquer Florida from the United States; Florida remained Spanish until 1819 by treaty.
option_explanations.C: Wrong. French-backed raids on New England belong to earlier colonial wars, not to Hamilton's post-Revolution complaint.
option_explanations.D: Wrong. The Dutch were not demanding tribute from American ships; the humiliation Hamilton described was Britain's, at the Great Lakes forts.

items.stem: Militiamen played a key Revolutionary War role by

stimulus.image_caption: Battle of Lexington, April 19, 1775 (after Amos Doolittle's 1775 engraving; U.S. National Archives).
stimulus.pd_rationale: After Amos Doolittle, 1775; U.S. National Archives
stimulus.stimulus_replacement: Questions 45-48 refer to the engraving above (replacing the bracketed description).

options: A. Routing British Regulars in battle
B. Sabotage and commando raids
C. Buying off Hessian contracts
D. Controlling populations beyond British reach
items.explanation: Militiamen rarely stood toe-to-toe with British regulars and won; their value was different. Operating in areas the British army could not reach or hold, local militias harassed supply lines, gathered intelligence, and — crucially — kept patriot authority alive among the population. By controlling the countryside beyond British reach, they denied the enemy the secure base a conventional victory required.

option_explanations.A: Wrong. Militia units seldom routed British regulars in open battle; that was the Continental Army's job.
option_explanations.B: Wrong. Sabotage and commando-style raids describe only a small part of militia activity, not their key strategic role.
option_explanations.C: Wrong. Militiamen did not buy off Hessian contracts; Hessians fought for Britain throughout the war.
option_explanations.D: Correct. The militia's key role was controlling populations and territory beyond British reach, sustaining the patriot cause where regulars could not.

items.stem: The Northwest Ordinance's organization of the Old Northwest as a national domain contributed to later problems primarily because the ordinance did which of the following?
options: (A) It ignored Native peoples' claims, setting the stage for violent conflict.
(B) It left the slavery question open, producing proslavery-antislavery violence.
(C) It made new states politically inferior to the original thirteen.
(D) It provided no mechanism for settlers to gain title to land.
items.explanation: The Northwest Ordinance organized the Old Northwest as national territory and set up an orderly path to statehood — but it simply ignored the Native peoples already living there. By treating their lands as empty national domain open to American settlement, it guaranteed collision. The result was decades of violent conflict in the Ohio Valley as settlers poured in and tribes resisted dispossession.

option_explanations.A: Correct. The ordinance ignored Native claims to the land, setting the stage for violent conflict as settlement advanced.
option_explanations.B: Wrong. The ordinance actually banned slavery in the Northwest Territory; the slavery question there was settled, not left open.
option_explanations.C: Wrong. The ordinance promised new states full equality with the original thirteen, not inferior status.
option_explanations.D: Wrong. The ordinance did provide mechanisms for surveying and selling land to settlers.

items.stem: The 'insurgents' Washington describes in the letter were primarily

stimulus.text:
The following questions refer to the excerpt below.

"I feel myself exceedingly obliged to you for the full & friendly communications in your letters... Commotions of this sort, like snow-balls, gather strength as they roll, if there is no opposition in the way to divide and crumble them."
—George Washington to Henry Knox on Shays's Rebellion, 1786 (abridged)

options: A. Debt-burdened farmers of western Massachusetts
B. British agents provocateurs sent to stir disorder
C. Urban merchants protesting trade restrictions
D. Enslaved people rising for their freedom
items.explanation: The insurgents Washington wrote about were the followers of Daniel Shays — debt-burdened farmers of western Massachusetts who rose up in 1786–1787. Crushed by taxes and debts after the Revolution, facing farm foreclosures and debtors' prison, they shut down courthouses to stop the seizures. Washington's alarm at their commotions was alarm at an uprising of indebted rural farmers.

option_explanations.A: Correct. The insurgents were debt-burdened western Massachusetts farmers — Shays's rebels — rising against foreclosures and crushing taxes.
option_explanations.B: Wrong. The rebellion was a homegrown uprising of indebted farmers, not a British plot; no agents provocateurs directed it.
option_explanations.C: Wrong. Urban merchants were not the insurgents; the rebels were rural farmers, and many merchants actually supported the government's crackdown.
option_explanations.D: Wrong. The Shays rebels were indebted white farmers, not enslaved people rising for freedom.

items.stem: The constitutional theory Calhoun advances in this passage is best known as which of the following?

stimulus.text: "If it be conceded... that the sovereign powers delegated are divided between the General and State Governments... it would seem impossible to deny to the States the right of deciding on the infractions of their powers, and the proper remedy to be applied for their correction.... to reserve such exclusive right to the General Government... is to convert it, in fact, into a great consolidated government, with unlimited powers, and to divest the States, in reality, of all their rights." — John C. Calhoun, 'South Carolina Exposition and Protest,' 1828

options: (A) Nullification: the claim that a state may declare a federal law void within its borders.
(B) The doctrine of implied powers.
(C) The gag rule against antislavery petitions.
(D) The American System of protective tariffs and internal improvements.
items.explanation: Calhoun's 1828 Exposition argues that since sovereign power is divided between the states and the federal government, the states must have the right to judge when the federal government oversteps — and to void the offending law within their borders. That is the doctrine of nullification, which South Carolina soon tried to apply to the tariff. The passage is the classic statement of the theory.

option_explanations.A: Correct. Calhoun's theory is nullification: a state may declare a federal law void within its borders.
option_explanations.B: Wrong. The doctrine of implied powers — associated with Hamilton and McCulloch v. Maryland — expands federal power, the opposite of Calhoun's argument.
option_explanations.C: Wrong. The gag rule (1836–1844) blocked antislavery petitions in the House; it is not a constitutional theory of state power.
option_explanations.D: Wrong. The American System of tariffs and internal improvements was Henry Clay's nationalist program — the very federal activism Calhoun was resisting.

items.stem: The Alamo's 'liberty or death' rhetoric most directly echoed

stimulus.pd_rationale: Painted 1844 by Theodore Gentilz. Pre-1930 publication; Public Domain tag confirmed (observed 2026-10-01).
stimulus.text_stimulus:
Questions 37–40 refer to the following quotation.

"Companions in arms! These remains which we have the honor of carrying on our shoulders are those of the valiant heroes who died in the Alamo. Yes, my friends, they preferred death to bondage..."
—Colonel Juan N. Seguin, oration, 1837 (abridged)

options: A. The Monroe Doctrine
B. Patrick Henry's 1775 'liberty or death' speech
C. The Nullification Crisis
D. The Seneca Falls Declaration
items.explanation: The defenders of the Alamo framed their stand as liberty or death — a deliberate echo of Patrick Henry's 1775 cry against British rule. The Texans saw themselves as heirs of the American Revolution, resisting what they portrayed as Mexican tyranny just as the patriots had resisted Britain's. The rhetoric linked their cause directly to the Revolutionary generation's language of freedom.

option_explanations.A: Wrong. The Monroe Doctrine (1823) warned Europe against colonizing the Americas; it had nothing to do with the Alamo's rhetoric.
option_explanations.B: Correct. The Alamo's liberty-or-death language directly echoed Patrick Henry's 1775 speech against British rule.
option_explanations.C: Wrong. The Nullification Crisis was about tariffs and states' rights in the 1830s, not the language of the Texas revolution.
option_explanations.D: Wrong. The Seneca Falls Declaration (1848) concerned women's rights, a different cause from the Alamo's.

items.stem: Jackson defends the removal policy in this passage primarily on which of the following grounds?

stimulus.text: "As a means of effecting this end I suggest for your consideration the propriety of setting apart an ample district west of the Mississippi, and without the limit of any State or Territory now formed, to be guaranteed to the Indian tribes as long as they shall occupy it. . . . This emigration would be voluntary, for it would be as cruel and unjust to compel the aborigines to abandon the graves of their fathers and seek a home in a distant land. But they should be distinctly informed that if they remain within the limits of the States they must be subject to their laws. . . ." — President Andrew Jackson, Address to Congress, 1829

options: (A) That the tribes themselves had petitioned for removal west of the Mississippi.
(B) That removal would enrich the federal treasury through land sales.
(C) That the Constitution explicitly required the removal of eastern tribes.
(D) That the emigration would be voluntary and would benefit the tribes by separating them from white settlement.
items.explanation: Jackson insists the removal would be voluntary — he calls forced removal cruel and unjust — and claims the policy benefits the tribes by moving them away from white settlement where, he says, they cannot survive. He frames removal as a humanitarian measure: separate the Indians from corrupting white contact and they will flourish. The reality proved very different, but this benevolent framing is the ground he defends in the passage.

option_explanations.A: Wrong. The tribes did not petition for removal; Jackson is proposing the policy, not responding to their request.
option_explanations.B: Wrong. Jackson does not defend removal as a way to enrich the treasury through land sales.
option_explanations.C: Wrong. The Constitution says nothing requiring the removal of eastern tribes; Jackson's argument is about policy, not constitutional mandate.
option_explanations.D: Correct. Jackson defends removal as voluntary and beneficial to the tribes, separating them from white settlement for their own good.

items.stem: [Image description: an 1828 lithograph of Sequoyah (George Guess), inventor of the Cherokee syllabary, shown in Western-style dress demonstrating his written characters.] The image best demonstrates which of the following?

stimulus.pd_rationale: Published 1838 (I. T. Bowen, Philadelphia; McKenney-Hall series). Pre-1930 publication; Public Domain tag confirmed on Commons file page (observed 2026-10-01).

options: (A) Cherokee determination to build a fully independent nation isolated from the United States.
(B) Cherokee defiance of laws banning schools on tribal lands.
(C) A Cherokee religious revival centered on traditional spiritual practices.
(D) Cherokee leaders' deliberate adoption of American cultural and political forms.
items.explanation: Sequoyah's syllabary — a written Cherokee language — shown alongside his Western-style dress, demonstrates how Cherokee leaders deliberately adopted American cultural and political forms. The Cherokee wrote a constitution, published a newspaper, and built schools modeled on American institutions. The image captures a strategy: prove the Cherokee a civilized nation by mastering the tools of the dominant culture.

option_explanations.A: Wrong. The Cherokee were not seeking isolation; they were engaging with American forms — a constitution, a press, written law — to defend their nationhood.
option_explanations.B: Wrong. The image shows cultural adoption, not defiance of school bans; the Cherokee built their own schools as part of that adoption.
option_explanations.C: Wrong. The syllabary was a linguistic and cultural achievement, not a religious revival centered on traditional spirituality.
option_explanations.D: Correct. The image demonstrates Cherokee leaders deliberately adopting American cultural and political forms.

items.stem: Which of the following is NOT true of the French historical situation leading to the event described in the excerpt?

stimulus.text: “The cession of Louisiana and the Floridas by Spain to France works most sorely on the U.S. On this subject the Secretary of State has written to you fully. Yet I cannot forbear recurring to it personally, so deep is the impression it makes in my mind. It completely reverses all the political relations of the U.S. and will form a new epoch in our political course. Of all nations of any consideration France is the one which hitherto has offered the fewest points on which we could have any conflict of right, and the most points of a communion of interests…. There is on the globe one single spot, the possessor of which is our natural and habitual enemy. It is New Orleans, through which the produce of three-eighths of our territory must pass to market, and from its fertility it will long yield more than half of our whole produce and contain more than half our inhabitants. France placing herself in that door assumes to us the attitude of defiance.” Source: Thomas Jefferson, a letter written to U.S. Ambassador (to France) Robert Livingston, 1802

options: (A) The city and port of New Orleans were too costly to continue to protect and maintain.
(B) The French needed money to raise armies and prepare for war on the European continent.
(C) Failure to arrest a slave revolt led to fears among European powers of similar uprisings throughout the New World.
(D) American exploration and expansionism would apply increasing pressure on the French colony.
items.explanation: Jefferson wrote this letter in 1802, when Spain had secretly returned Louisiana to France. France's decision to sell came from its own circumstances: Napoleon needed money for his European wars, the Haitian slave revolt had destroyed France's most valuable colony and its American ambitions, and American westward pressure was growing. What is NOT true is that New Orleans was too costly for France to protect and maintain — France gave it up for strategic and financial reasons, not because the port was a maintenance burden.

option_explanations.A: Correct — this is the NOT true statement. France did not sell Louisiana because New Orleans was too costly to maintain; it sold because of war needs, Haiti, and American pressure.
option_explanations.B: This is true, so it is not the answer. Napoleon needed funds for his European wars, which pushed him to sell Louisiana.
option_explanations.C: This is true, so it is not the answer. The Haitian slave revolt's success alarmed Europeans and ended Napoleon's dream of an American empire.
option_explanations.D: This is true, so it is not the answer. Growing American expansionism put increasing pressure on the French colony.

items.stem: All of the following are true of early New England textile mills EXCEPT

stimulus.pd_rationale: Published 1845. Pre-1930 publication; Public Domain tag confirmed (observed 2026-10-01).

options: A. Women made up much of their workforce
B. They depended on water power
C. They organized work through the putting-out system
D. Labor unrest was rare before the 1830s
items.explanation: Early New England mills — like Lowell's — employed young farm women as their main workforce, ran on water power from rivers, and saw little labor unrest before the 1830s. What they did not use was the putting-out system, in which merchants distributed raw materials to workers in their own homes. The mills replaced that home-based system with centralized factory production under one roof.

option_explanations.A: This is true of the mills, so it is not the answer. Young women — the famous Lowell mill girls — made up much of the workforce.
option_explanations.B: This is true of the mills, so it is not the answer. They depended on water power from New England rivers.
option_explanations.C: Correct — this is the EXCEPT. The mills used centralized factory production, not the home-based putting-out system they replaced.
option_explanations.D: This is true of the mills, so it is not the answer. Serious labor unrest came later, in the 1830s and beyond.

items.stem: All of the following resulted from the policy referenced in the cartoon above EXCEPT

stimulus.text: King Andrew the First , Unknown Artist, c. 1833

options: (A) the depositing of federal funds in state banks
(B) land over-speculation and a massive financial panic
(C) a permanent end to federalized central banking
(D) the invigoration of a political party opposed to Jackson’s financial policies
items.explanation: The King Andrew the First cartoon attacks Jackson's war on the Bank of the United States. Jackson's veto and removal of federal deposits into state pet banks did produce deposit shifts, land speculation, the Panic of 1837, and a new Whig opposition organized against his financial policies. What did not happen was a permanent end to central banking — the United States eventually created the Federal Reserve in 1913. Jackson killed the Second Bank, not the idea of central banking forever.

option_explanations.A: This did result from the policy, so it is not the answer. Jackson moved federal funds into state pet banks.
option_explanations.B: This did result from the policy, so it is not the answer. Speculation fueled by easy credit helped bring on the Panic of 1837.
option_explanations.C: Correct — this is the EXCEPT. Central banking was not ended permanently; the Federal Reserve was established in 1913.
option_explanations.D: This did result from the policy, so it is not the answer. Opposition to Jackson's bank war helped forge the Whig Party.

items.stem: Anthony delivered this argument in 1873 most directly in response to which of the following?

stimulus.text: "One-half of the people of this nation today are utterly powerless to blot from the statute books an unjust law, or to write there a new and a just one. The women, dissatisfied as they are with this form of government, that enforces taxation without representation,—that compels them to obey laws to which they have never given their consent,—that imprisons and hangs them without a trial by a jury of their peers, that robs them, in marriage, of the custody of their own persons, wages and children,—are this half of the people left wholly at the mercy of the other half, in direct violation of the spirit and letter of the declarations of the framers of this government, every one of which was based on the immutable principle of equal rights to all." — Susan B. Anthony, 'I Stand Before You Under Indictment,' 1873

options: (A) The Seneca Falls Convention of 1848.
(B) The ratification of the Nineteenth Amendment.
(C) Her arrest and trial for voting in the 1872 presidential election.
(D) The passage of the Fifteenth Amendment.
items.explanation: Susan B. Anthony delivered this speech in 1873 after being arrested, tried, and convicted for voting in the 1872 presidential election. She had voted to test whether the Fourteenth Amendment's guarantees covered women, and her indictment gave her a national platform. The speech's fury — taxation without representation, laws made without women's consent — is her direct answer to the prosecution that put her on trial for casting a ballot.

option_explanations.A: Wrong. The Seneca Falls Convention was 1848, twenty-five years earlier; this 1873 speech responds to her own trial.
option_explanations.B: Wrong. The Nineteenth Amendment was ratified in 1920, nearly fifty years after this speech.
option_explanations.C: Correct. Anthony spoke in direct response to her arrest and trial for voting in the 1872 election.
option_explanations.D: Wrong. The Fifteenth Amendment (1870) enfranchised Black men; Anthony's speech concerns women's exclusion, sparked by her prosecution.

items.stem: Reconstruction ended with the Compromise of 1877 because

stimulus.pd_rationale: Original diagram generated by the committed fixed-seed script gen_election_maps.py (this directory). No third-party source; electoral data cross-checked against published state-by-state results.

options: A. A presidential order ended it
B. Federal troops were withdrawn from the South
C. Hayes personally opposed Reconstruction
D. Black political power made it unnecessary
items.explanation: The Compromise of 1877 settled the disputed 1876 presidential election: Democrats accepted Republican Rutherford B. Hayes as president in exchange for the withdrawal of the last federal troops from the South. With the troops gone, Reconstruction's enforcement collapsed — Republican state governments fell and white Democrats reclaimed power. The troop withdrawal was the mechanism that ended Reconstruction.

option_explanations.A: Wrong. No presidential order ended Reconstruction; it ended through the political bargain that removed federal troops.
option_explanations.B: Correct. The Compromise of 1877 withdrew federal troops from the South, and without them Reconstruction could not survive.
option_explanations.C: Wrong. Hayes accepted the bargain, but the cause was the deal itself — troop withdrawal — not his personal opposition.
option_explanations.D: Wrong. Black political power was being violently suppressed, not making Reconstruction unnecessary; its loss was the tragedy of the compromise.

items.stem: The court case referenced in the source above upheld which of the following principles?

stimulus.text: “In one view the slaveholders have a decided advantage over all opposition. It is well to notice this advantage—the advantage of complete organization. They are organized; and yet were not at the pains of creating their organizations. The State governments, where the system of slavery exists, are complete slavery organizations. The church organizations in those States are equally at the service of slavery; while the Federal Government, with its army and navy, from the chief magistracy in Washington, to the Supreme Court, and thence to the chief marshalship at New York, is pledged to support, defend, and propagate the crying curse of human bondage. The pen, the purse, and the sword, are united against the simple truth, preached by humble men in obscure places.” Source: Frederick Douglass, “The Dred Scott Decision” (speech), 1857 (public domain).

options: (A) The existence of “separate but equal” facilities for people of different races was constitutional.
(B) Corporations were entitled to the same protections guaranteed to individuals under the Fourteenth Amendment.
(C) School prayer violated the principle of “separation of church and state.”
(D) Congress had no right to regulate slavery in United States territories.
items.explanation: Frederick Douglass's 1857 speech attacks the Dred Scott decision, in which the Supreme Court ruled that Congress had no power to ban slavery in the territories — effectively declaring the Missouri Compromise unconstitutional. Douglass describes a system where every institution, from state governments to the Supreme Court, is organized to defend slavery. The principle the case upheld was congressional powerlessness over slavery in the territories.

option_explanations.A: Wrong. Separate but equal came from Plessy v. Ferguson (1896), not Dred Scott.
option_explanations.B: Wrong. Corporate personhood under the Fourteenth Amendment developed in later cases, not in Dred Scott.
option_explanations.C: Wrong. School prayer and the separation of church and state were twentieth-century issues, not 1857 ones.
option_explanations.D: Correct. The Dred Scott decision upheld the principle that Congress had no right to regulate slavery in the territories.

items.stem: Which of the following was an immediate consequence of the secession of South Carolina?

stimulus.pd_rationale: Original diagram generated by the committed fixed-seed script gen_election_maps.py (this directory). No third-party source; secession dates are the standard ordinance dates.
stimulus.text_stimulus: “On the 4th day of March next, this party will take possession of the Government. It has announced that…a war must be waged against slavery until it shall cease throughout the United States. “The guaranties of the Constitution will then no longer exist; the equal rights of the States will be lost. The slave-holding States will no longer have the power of self-government, or self-protection, and the Federal Government will have become their enemy. “Sectional interest and animosity will deepen the irritation, and all hope of remedy is rendered vain, by the fact that public opinion at the North has invested a great political error with the sanction of more erroneous religious belief. We, therefore, the People of South Carolina…have solemnly declared that the Union heretofore existing between this State and the other States of North America, is dissolved, and that the State of South Carolina has resumed her position among the nations of the world, as a separate and independent State.” Source: “Declaration of the Immediate Causes Which Induce and Justify the Secession of South Carolina from the Federal Union,” 1860

options: (A) Southern Democrats appealed to the powers of Congress to stop military action against South Carolina.
(B) Abraham Lincoln signed the Emancipation Proclamation.
(C) Other southern states seceded from the Union, forming the Confederacy.
(D) Jefferson Davis drafted Confederate soldiers into war, defending the siege on Fort Sumter.
items.explanation: South Carolina seceded in December 1860, and its example was immediately followed: Mississippi, Florida, Alabama, Georgia, Louisiana, and Texas seceded in the next six weeks, forming the Confederate States of America in February 1861. Secession was contagious — one state's break gave the others political cover to follow. The immediate consequence was not war or emancipation but the rapid formation of a Southern confederacy.

option_explanations.A: Wrong. Southern Democrats did not appeal to Congress to stop military action; they were leaving Congress to form their own government.
option_explanations.B: Wrong. Lincoln signed the Emancipation Proclamation in 1863, two years after secession began.
option_explanations.C: Correct. South Carolina's secession was immediately followed by other Southern states seceding and forming the Confederacy.
option_explanations.D: Wrong. Fort Sumter was attacked in April 1861, months after secession; Davis did not draft soldiers to defend a siege at this stage.

items.stem: [Data: an 1855 New York State census table of Irish-born workers in New York City — e.g., 23,386 Irish domestic servants (74% of all domestic servants), 17,426 laborers (86% of all laborers), 1,758 laundresses (69%), alongside much smaller Irish shares in skilled trades and almost none in professions (113 doctors, 40 lawyers).] Which factor was the most important cause of the migration pattern shown in this table?
options: (A) British persecution driving Irish political dissidents into exile.
(B) Rapid mechanization of Irish agriculture displacing the rural workforce.
(C) A catastrophic potato famine that destroyed Ireland's staple crop.
(D) A new New York religious-toleration law welcoming Irish Catholics.
items.explanation: The table shows Irish immigrants concentrated in domestic service and unskilled labor — the jobs open to desperately poor newcomers. The cause was the Great Famine of the late 1840s: the potato blight destroyed Ireland's staple crop, starving a million people and driving another million-plus across the Atlantic. These were refugees from hunger, arriving with nothing and taking whatever work they could get.

option_explanations.A: Wrong. The migrants were famine refugees, not political dissidents exiled by British persecution.
option_explanations.B: Wrong. Mechanization of Irish agriculture was not the driver; the potato blight's destruction of the food supply was.
option_explanations.C: Correct. The catastrophic potato famine destroyed Ireland's staple crop and drove the migration shown in the table.
option_explanations.D: Wrong. No New York toleration law caused this migration; hunger and survival did.

items.stem: Copperheads were

stimulus.pd_rationale: Published 1864 (Library of Congress). Pre-1930 publication; Public Domain tag confirmed (observed 2026-10-01).

options: A. Northern Democrats who opposed the war
B. Northern Republicans who wanted Lincoln replaced
C. Northern Democrats who rallied to Lincoln
D. Southern Democrats seeking early negotiations
items.explanation: Copperheads were Northern Democrats who opposed the Civil War and demanded an immediate negotiated peace with the Confederacy. Named for the venomous snake by their Republican enemies, they denounced Lincoln's war measures — emancipation, conscription, the suspension of habeas corpus — as tyrannical. Their strength in the Midwest made them Lincoln's most bitter Northern opponents.

option_explanations.A: Correct. Copperheads were Northern Democrats who opposed the war and demanded a negotiated peace.
option_explanations.B: Wrong. Republicans who wanted Lincoln replaced were Radical Republicans, not Copperheads.
option_explanations.C: Wrong. Copperheads denounced Lincoln; Northern Democrats who rallied to him were War Democrats, a different faction.
option_explanations.D: Wrong. Copperheads were Northerners, not Southerners, and they opposed the war rather than seeking negotiations from the Southern side.

items.stem: Reports like this one from Freedmen's Bureau officials most directly contributed to which of the following?

stimulus.text: "Wherever I go — the street, the shop, the house, or the steamboat — I hear the people talk in such a way as to indicate that they are yet unable to conceive of the Negro as possessing any rights at all. Men who are honorable in their dealings with their white neighbors will cheat a Negro without feeling a single twinge of their honor. To kill a Negro they do not deem murder; to debauch a Negro woman they do not think fornication; to take the property away from a Negro they do not consider robbery. . . . The whites esteem the blacks their property by natural right, and however much they may admit that the individual relations of masters and slaves have been destroyed by the war and the President's emancipation proclamation, they still have an ingrained feeling that the blacks at large belong to the whites at large." — Col. Samuel Thomas, Assistant Commissioner, Bureau of Refugees, Freedmen and Abandoned Lands, testimony before Congress, 1865

options: (A) The immediate abolition of the Freedmen's Bureau.
(B) The voluntary enfranchisement of Black men by Southern states.
(C) Congressional Reconstruction, including the Civil Rights Act of 1866.
(D) The Supreme Court's Dred Scott decision.
items.explanation: Colonel Thomas's 1865 testimony painted a South where whites still treated Black people as property in every practical sense — cheated, killed, and robbed without consequence. Such reports convinced Congress that presidential Reconstruction was failing and that only federal power could secure freedpeople's rights. The direct result was Congressional Reconstruction: the Civil Rights Act of 1866, the Fourteenth Amendment, and military rule in the South.

option_explanations.A: Wrong. Congress expanded the Freedmen's Bureau's powers and funding; it did not abolish it in response to these reports.
option_explanations.B: Wrong. Southern states did not voluntarily enfranchise Black men; Congress had to impose Black suffrage through Reconstruction.
option_explanations.C: Correct. Reports of Southern intransigence drove Congress to seize control of Reconstruction, passing the Civil Rights Act of 1866 and related measures.
option_explanations.D: Wrong. The Dred Scott decision was 1857, eight years before this 1865 testimony.

items.stem: Land-grant colleges' emphasis on agriculture and mechanics most directly served the Republican ideal of

stimulus.text:
Questions 53–55 refer to the following quotation.

"Be it enacted ... That there be granted to the several States, for the purposes hereinafter mentioned, an amount of public land, to be apportioned to each State a quantity equal to thirty thousand acres for each senator and representative..."
—Morrill Land-Grant Act, 1862 (abridged)

options: A. Plantation agriculture
B. Free labor — dignified work open to all
C. Industrial monopoly
D. Economic isolation from world markets
items.explanation: The Morrill Act's land-grant colleges taught agriculture and the mechanic arts — practical, hands-on work — because Republicans believed in the dignity of free labor. Their ideal was a society where ordinary people rose by their own productive effort, not one of plantations worked by slaves or monopolies worked by wage slaves. Colleges for farmers and mechanics embodied the free-labor vision: work open to all, dignified in itself.

option_explanations.A: Wrong. Plantation agriculture was the slave system Republicans opposed; land-grant colleges served the opposite ideal.
option_explanations.B: Correct. Agricultural and mechanical colleges served the Republican ideal of free labor — dignified work open to all.
option_explanations.C: Wrong. Industrial monopoly was what Republicans' free-labor ideology stood against, not for.
option_explanations.D: Wrong. Economic isolation was never a Republican goal; the party favored internal development within an active commercial nation.

items.stem: Nation's saloon-smashing as political theater most directly parallels which other Progressive Era tactic?

stimulus.text:
Questions 49–52 refer to the following quotation.

"I arrived at Wichita the 28th, the raid was postponed until the 29th. I took hatchets with me and we also supplied ourselves with rocks, meeting at the church, where we sang and prayed before smashing the saloon..."
—Carry A. Nation, on her saloon raids, 1900 (abridged)

options: A. Woman suffrage parades and White House pickets
B. Settlement-house work
C. Scientific management studies
D. The conservation movement
items.explanation: Carry Nation turned saloon-smashing into a public spectacle — praying, singing, and swinging her hatchet before crowds and cameras — to force the nation to talk about prohibition. Woman suffragists used the same logic: parades down Fifth Avenue and silent pickets outside the White House were staged confrontations designed for publicity, not private persuasion. Both tactics used dramatic public theater to make an ignored cause impossible to ignore.

option_explanations.A: Correct. Suffrage parades and White House pickets, like Nation's raids, used staged public spectacle to draw press attention to a cause.
option_explanations.B: Wrong. Settlement-house work was quiet neighborhood social service, not confrontational public theater.
option_explanations.C: Wrong. Scientific management studies were efficiency analyses of factories, not publicity tactics.
option_explanations.D: Wrong. The conservation movement worked through policy and preserves, not through staged dramatic confrontations.

items.stem: The cartoon's criticism of Carnegie is best summarized as

stimulus.pd_rationale: Published 1892 (pre-1930); Public domain tag on Wikimedia Commons file page.
stimulus.text_stimulus: Image description: 'Forty-Millionaire Carnegie in his Great Double Role,' The Saturday Globe, July 9, 1892 — a cartoon portraying Andrew Carnegie in two contrasting roles: the generous philanthropist dispensing charity, and the industrialist profiting from the harsh treatment of his workers.

options: (A) His philanthropy was funded by violating his workers' rights.
(B) He gave too little of his fortune to charitable causes.
(C) He divided his attention and succeeded at neither philanthropy nor business.
(D) His ruthless business practices had severed his ties to his working-class origins.
items.explanation: The cartoon attacks Carnegie for giving away libraries and concert halls with money squeezed from his workers — most notoriously at Homestead in 1892, where his company crushed the steelworkers' union with Pinkerton violence and wage cuts. The criticism is that his philanthropy was built on broken strikes, twelve-hour days, and suppressed wages. The giving does not cleanse the getting.

option_explanations.A: Correct. The cartoon charges that Carnegie's philanthropy was funded by violating his workers' rights — low wages, long hours, crushed unions.
option_explanations.B: Wrong. The cartoon does not complain he gave too little; it attacks the source of what he gave.
option_explanations.C: Wrong. The cartoon does not suggest he failed at both; it contrasts his celebrated giving with his ruthless labor practices.
option_explanations.D: Wrong. The point is not that he forgot his working-class origins but that his charity rested on workers' suffering.

items.stem: Sumner's claim that 'the millionaires are a product of natural selection' drew most directly on which of the following?

stimulus.text: "A drunkard in the gutter is just where he ought to be.... The law of survival of the fittest was not made by man, and it cannot be abrogated by man.... The millionaires are a product of natural selection.... Let one of them make a mistake and see how quickly the concentration gives way to dispersion." — William Graham Sumner, What Social Classes Owe to Each Other, 1883

options: (A) Adam Smith's labor theory of value.
(B) Karl Marx's theory of class struggle.
(C) Charles Darwin's theory of evolution, applied to human society as Social Darwinism.
(D) The Social Gospel movement.
items.explanation: Sumner's language — survival of the fittest, natural selection — comes straight from Charles Darwin's theory of evolution, which Sumner and others applied to human society as Social Darwinism. The argument was that economic winners deserved their wealth because nature selected them, and helping the poor would interfere with natural law. It gave industrial-era inequality a scientific-sounding justification.

option_explanations.A: Wrong. Adam Smith wrote about markets and the division of labor, not about natural selection producing millionaires.
option_explanations.B: Wrong. Marx's class-struggle theory condemned millionaires as exploiters — the opposite of Sumner's celebration of them.
option_explanations.C: Correct. Sumner drew on Darwin's theory of evolution, recast as Social Darwinism to justify wealth as nature's verdict.
option_explanations.D: Wrong. The Social Gospel movement demanded Christians help the poor; Sumner argued the poor deserved their fate.

items.stem: Which best describes the West in the 25 years after the Civil War?

stimulus.pd_rationale: Photograph by A. J. Russell, 1869 (pre-1930); Public domain tag on Commons.
stimulus.text_stimulus:
Questions 6–8 refer to the illustration described below.

The famous 1869 photograph of the Golden Spike ceremony at Promontory Summit, Utah: two locomotives face each other, their cowcatchers nearly touching, while railroad workers, officials, and a military band crowd around the tracks where the final spike joins the Union Pacific and Central Pacific lines.

options: A. The West stayed largely unexplored wilderness
B. The frontier rapidly disappeared
C. The U.S. seized new lands from Mexico and Britain
D. The West became a manufacturing center
items.explanation: In the quarter-century after the Civil War, railroads, mining, cattle ranching, and homesteading transformed the West with stunning speed. The Census Bureau declared the frontier line closed in 1890 — the unsettled wilderness had been carved into farms, towns, and territories. The era's defining feature was not enduring wilderness but the frontier's rapid disappearance.

option_explanations.A: Wrong. The West did not stay unexplored wilderness; railroads and settlement penetrated it within a generation.
option_explanations.B: Correct. The frontier rapidly disappeared as railroads, mining, ranching, and farming settled the West after the Civil War.
option_explanations.C: Wrong. No major seizures of Mexican or British land occurred in this period; the continental map was essentially set.
option_explanations.D: Wrong. The West remained agricultural and extractive; manufacturing stayed concentrated in the Northeast and Midwest.

items.stem: Which of the following was an accomplishment of the political movement behind sentiments like these?
options: (A) Establishing a federal minimum wage.
(B) Winning state laws regulating railroad rates and practices.
(C) Moving U.S. currency from the gold standard to the silver standard.
(D) Creating a permanent federal price-support system for small farmers.
items.explanation: The agrarian movement behind these sentiments — the Granger movement of the 1870s — turned farmers' anger at railroad monopolies into political action. Its concrete achievement was winning state laws regulating railroad rates and practices: the Granger Laws, upheld in Munn v. Illinois (1877), which let states cap the charges of grain elevators and railroads. Farmers learned they could use state power against corporate power.

option_explanations.A: Wrong. A federal minimum wage did not arrive until the Fair Labor Standards Act of 1938, far beyond this movement's era.
option_explanations.B: Correct. The movement won state laws regulating railroad rates and practices — the Granger Laws.
option_explanations.C: Wrong. The movement never moved the currency off the gold standard; the silver fight belonged to the later Populists.
option_explanations.D: Wrong. Permanent federal farm price supports came with the New Deal, not with the 1870s agrarian movement.

items.stem: Addams's account suggests that the striking girls' vulnerability came mainly from

stimulus.pd_rationale: Vintage V.O. Hammon (Chicago) postcard of Hull House, early 1900s; Public domain tag on Commons.
stimulus.text_stimulus:
Questions 1–4 refer to the following quotation.

"At a meeting of working girls held at Hull House during a strike in a large shoe factory, the discussions made it clear that the strikers who had been most easily frightened were those who had no one to stand by them..."
—Jane Addams, Twenty Years at Hull House, 1910 (abridged)

options: A. Their lack of formal education
B. Their dependence on employers and landlords for housing
C. Federal strikebreaking injunctions
D. Their recent arrival as immigrants
items.explanation: Jane Addams observed that the young women strikers were trapped by their living arrangements: many depended on their employers or on company-tied landlords for the roofs over their heads. Going on strike meant risking not just wages but shelter itself. That dependence — on the boss for both paycheck and housing — is what made the girls so vulnerable when they walked out.

option_explanations.A: Wrong. Addams locates their vulnerability in their economic dependence, not in their level of schooling.
option_explanations.B: Correct. The striking girls' vulnerability came from depending on employers and landlords for housing — striking risked homelessness as well as joblessness.
option_explanations.C: Wrong. Federal strikebreaking injunctions were a later and different weapon, not the source of vulnerability Addams describes.
option_explanations.D: Wrong. Addams's point is about their dependence on employers for shelter, not about how recently they immigrated.

items.stem: The organization that gave farmers' views the largest national audience was the
options: A. Greenback Party
B. Populist Party
C. The Grange
D. Farmers' Alliances
items.explanation: The Grange and the Farmers' Alliances organized farmers regionally, and the Greenback Party carried some of their ideas, but only the Populist Party — the People's Party of 1892 — gave farmers a national political stage. Its presidential campaigns, its Omaha platform, and its fusion with the Democrats in 1896 broadcast agrarian grievances to the entire country. No farm organization reached a larger national audience.

option_explanations.A: Wrong. The Greenback Party was a smaller, earlier currency-reform party with a narrower reach.
option_explanations.B: Correct. The Populist Party gave farmers' views their largest national audience through presidential campaigns and a national platform.
option_explanations.C: Wrong. The Grange was important but primarily a social and lobbying organization, not a national electoral vehicle.
option_explanations.D: Wrong. The Farmers' Alliances built the movement's base, but the Populist Party carried its message nationally.

items.stem: Republican leaders of the 1920s believed all of the following EXCEPT
options: A. 'The business of government is business'
B. Government should do as little as possible
C. Labor unions should be strengthened by law
D. Immigration should remain restricted
items.explanation: Republican leaders of the 1920s — Harding, Coolidge, Hoover — preached that the business of government is business, that government should do as little as possible, and they kept immigration restricted through the quota acts. What they did not believe was that labor unions should be strengthened by law; they used injunctions and prosecutions against unions instead. Strengthening unions by statute was the New Deal's project, not theirs.

option_explanations.A: Republicans did believe this, so it is not the answer. Coolidge's dictum made business the government's business.
option_explanations.B: Republicans did believe this, so it is not the answer. Minimal government interference was their creed.
option_explanations.C: Correct — this is the EXCEPT. 1920s Republicans opposed unions and used courts against them; strengthening unions by law came later.
option_explanations.D: Republicans did believe this, so it is not the answer. They kept the restrictive immigration quotas of the 1920s.

items.stem: Which of the following groups would likely be most supportive of policies created in response to the situation depicted above after 1933?

stimulus.source_page: Generated original — see charts/gen_unemployment_1929_1941.py (fixed-seed matplotlib script).
stimulus.pd_rationale: Original chart; data are BLS historical annual unemployment rates 1929-1941 (facts, not copyrightable); no copyrighted source reproduced.
stimulus.text_stimulus: [Described graph — U.S. unemployment rate, 1929–1941 (public-domain style statistical chart; original artwork not reproduced). Unemployment spikes after the 1929 crash and peaks around 1933 at roughly one-quarter of the workforce. It then generally declines through the mid-1930s, rises again during the 1937–1938 downturn, and remains elevated near the end of the decade; a full recovery coincides with U.S. entry into World War II.]

options: (A) Industrial business owners
(B) African American agricultural workers
(C) Critics of American involvement in European affairs
(D) Labor union organizers
items.explanation: After 1933, the New Deal answered the Depression's devastation of workers with pro-labor policies: the Wagner Act protecting collective bargaining, public works jobs, and Social Security. The natural supporters of that response were labor union organizers, who gained legal recognition and a surge of membership. The crisis of workers became the opening for organized labor's greatest advances.

option_explanations.A: Wrong. Industrial business owners generally opposed New Deal labor policies as government interference.
option_explanations.B: Wrong. African American agricultural workers were largely excluded from early New Deal labor protections, which often omitted farm and domestic workers.
option_explanations.C: Wrong. Critics of foreign involvement focused on neutrality, not on domestic labor policy.
option_explanations.D: Correct. Labor union organizers were the natural supporters of the New Deal's pro-labor response to the Depression.

items.stem: The sentiment expressed by Beveridge best exemplifies which of the following?

stimulus.text: “The Opposition tells us that we ought not to govern a people without their consent. I answer, the rule of liberty that all just government derives its authority from the consent of the governed, applies only to those who are capable of self-government. We govern the Indians without their consent, we govern our territories without their consent, we govern our children without their consent. How do they know that our government would be without their consent? Would not the people of the Philippines prefer the just, human, civilizing government of this Republic to the savage, bloody rule of pillage and extortion from which we have rescued them? And, regardless of this formula of words made only for enlightened, self-governing people, do we owe no duty to the world? Shall we turn these peoples back to the reeking hands from which we have taken them? Shall we abandon them, with Germany, England, Japan, hungering for them? Shall we save them from those nations, to give them a self-rule of tragedy?…Then like men and not like children, let us on to our tasks, our mission, and our destiny.” Source: Albert J. Beveridge, “The March of the Flag,” 1898

options: (A) Imperialism
(B) Anti-imperialism
(C) Isolationism
(D) Manifest Destiny
items.explanation: Beveridge's March of the Flag is a full-throated defense of American imperialism: the United States should govern the Philippines because Filipinos are incapable of self-government and because America has a civilizing mission. He dismisses consent of the governed as a formula for enlightened peoples only and calls empire America's task and destiny. The speech is the classic statement of the imperialist case in 1898.

option_explanations.A: Correct. Beveridge's speech exemplifies imperialism — the argument that America should rule foreign peoples as a civilizing mission.
option_explanations.B: Wrong. Anti-imperialists opposed exactly what Beveridge celebrates; they argued empire betrayed American principles.
option_explanations.C: Wrong. Isolationism means avoiding foreign entanglements; Beveridge demands America take up global rule.
option_explanations.D: Wrong. Manifest Destiny concerned continental expansion in the 1840s; Beveridge argues for overseas empire in 1898.

items.stem: The 1899 cartoon makes the point that

stimulus.pd_rationale: 1899 photograph (pre-1930); Public domain tag on Commons; LOC print.
stimulus.text_stimulus: Image description: William Carson, 'A Bigger Job Than He Thought For,' Sunday Globe (Utica, NY), 1899 — a cartoon showing Uncle Sam struggling to manage a large, unruly child labeled 'Philippines,' suggesting the difficulty of governing the islands acquired after the Spanish-American War.

options: (A) insurgents in Cuba were being manipulated by Spain into resisting the presence of American troops.
(B) native Hawaiians behaved childishly when the United States annexed Hawaii.
(C) the United States misjudged the Filipino response to American control.
(D) building the Panama Canal proved slower and costlier than expected.
items.explanation: The 1899 cartoon satirizes American overconfidence after annexing the Philippines: Washington expected gratitude and easy rule, but Filipinos — who had fought Spain for independence — rose in bloody revolt instead. The cartoon's point is the misjudgment: Americans assumed their flag would be welcomed and discovered they had bought a war. Imperial fantasy collided with Filipino nationalism.

option_explanations.A: Wrong. The cartoon is about the Philippines and American misjudgment, not about Spain manipulating Cuban insurgents.
option_explanations.B: Wrong. Hawaii's annexation is not the cartoon's subject; the point concerns the Filipino response.
option_explanations.C: Correct. The cartoon makes the point that the United States misjudged how Filipinos would respond to American control.
option_explanations.D: Wrong. The Panama Canal project is unrelated to this 1899 cartoon's argument.

items.stem: McPherson's national prominence illustrates which 1920s development?

stimulus.text:
The following questions refer to the excerpt below.

Reviewing Aimee Semple McPherson's autobiography, Dorothy Parker archly treats the celebrity evangelist's book as show business — entertaining, sensational, and revealing how thoroughly religion, like everything else in the 1920s, had become a form of mass entertainment.
—After Dorothy Parker's review of McPherson's This Is That, 1920s

options: A. The decline of all religious observance in America
B. The triumph of mainline churches over revivalism
C. The end of women's public religious roles
D. The rise of mass media that turned preachers into celebrities
items.explanation: Aimee Semple McPherson built a religious empire in 1920s Los Angeles with radio broadcasts, theatrical stage productions, and relentless publicity — she was as much a media personality as a preacher. Dorothy Parker's review treats her book as show business because that is what her ministry had become. Her prominence illustrates how mass media — radio, newspapers, celebrity culture — turned preachers into national celebrities.

option_explanations.A: Wrong. Religious observance did not decline across the board; McPherson drew enormous crowds.
option_explanations.B: Wrong. McPherson was a flamboyant revivalist outsider, not a triumph of staid mainline churches.
option_explanations.C: Wrong. McPherson's career proved the opposite: women could command huge public religious roles.
option_explanations.D: Correct. McPherson's fame illustrates the rise of mass media that turned preachers into celebrities.

items.stem: In contrast to Roosevelt’s Square Deal, FDR’s First New Deal program aimed to

stimulus.text: “It is not enough to be well-meaning and kindly, but weak; neither is it enough to be strong, unless morality and decency go hand in hand with strength. We must possess the qualities which make us do our duty in our homes and among our neighbors, and in addition we must possess the qualities which are indispensable to the make-up of every great and masterful nation—the qualities of courage and hardihood, of individual initiative and yet of power to combine for a common end, and above all, the resolute determination to permit no man and no set of men to sunder us one from the other by lines of caste or creed or section. We must act upon the motto of all for each and each for all. There must be ever present in our minds the fundamental truth that in a republic such as ours the only safety is to stand neither for nor against any man because he is rich or because he is poor, because he is engaged in one occupation or another, because he works with his brains or because he works with his hands. We must treat each man on his worth and merits as a man. We must see that each is given a square deal, because he is entitled to no more and should receive no less.” Source: Theodore Roosevelt, a speech to farmers in New York, 1903

options: (A) improve crumbling domestic infrastructure
(B) provide work and stabilize the labor force
(C) restore confidence in the economy and banking system
(D) ensure financial support for retired and disabled workers
items.explanation: Theodore Roosevelt's Square Deal promised fairness between labor and capital, but Franklin Roosevelt's First New Deal faced a different emergency: a collapsed banking system and an economy frozen by fear. Its first moves — the bank holiday, the Emergency Banking Act, fireside chats urging Americans to trust the banks — aimed above all to restore confidence in the economy and the banking system. Stabilization came before reform.

option_explanations.A: Wrong. Infrastructure work came with later programs; the First New Deal's priority was financial confidence.
option_explanations.B: Wrong. Providing work mattered, but the opening and defining aim was restoring faith in banks and the economy.
option_explanations.C: Correct. The First New Deal aimed first to restore confidence in the economy and banking system — the bank holiday and fireside chats.
option_explanations.D: Wrong. Support for retired and disabled workers came with the Second New Deal's Social Security Act of 1935.

items.stem: Cohen's account best helps explain which of the following political developments?

stimulus.text: How industrial workers in one American city lived through an era when the nation shifted from relying on private welfare capitalism to building a welfare state — and from fighting the organization of its industrial workforce to accepting it. — paraphrased from Lizabeth Cohen, Making a New Deal: Industrial Workers in Chicago, 1919–1939 (1990)

options: (A) A sharp decline in voter turnout during the 1930s.
(B) The rise of a Republican majority in the Sunbelt states.
(C) The passage of the Taft-Hartley Act.
(D) The emergence of a durable Democratic majority anchored by urban industrial workers.
items.explanation: Lizabeth Cohen shows how Chicago's industrial workers — battered by the Depression, organized by the CIO, and aided by New Deal labor law — moved from suspicion of government to reliance on it, and from anti-union workplaces to organized ones. That transformation built the Roosevelt coalition: urban industrial workers became the anchor of a Democratic majority that dominated national politics for decades.

option_explanations.A: Wrong. Voter turnout did not sharply decline in the 1930s; the Depression politicized workers and turnout held.
